questions.q: Which school, founded in 1919, sought to bridge the gap between 'Fine Arts' and 'Applied Arts' to create a 'Total Work of Art' (Gesamtkunstwerk)?
questions.n: Founded by Walter Gropius in Weimar, it revolutionized 20th-century design by merging craftsmanship with industrial mass production.

questions.q: What was the name of the prestigious French school that emphasized academic classicism and 'Grand Prix' competitions?
questions.n: This institution dictated the 'Grand Manner' of architecture, emphasizing symmetry, hierarchy, and classical ornamentation.

questions.q: Which Russian school, contemporary to the Bauhaus, was the center for Constructivism and focused on technical workshops?
questions.n: Often called the 'Russian Bauhaus,' it was a state art and technical school that explored avant-garde concepts in Moscow.

questions.q: What is the name of the American art colony and school in Michigan, designed by Eliel Saarinen, known as the 'Cradle of Mid-Century Modernism'?
questions.n: Many icons of Modernism, like Charles Eames and Florence Knoll, studied or taught here under Saarinen's leadership.

questions.q: Which design movement/school in late 19th-century Britain, led by William Morris, reacted against industrialization by promoting hand-craftsmanship?
questions.n: Morris and his followers advocated for the dignity of the laborer and the inherent beauty of handmade goods over machine-made items.

questions.q: Before founding the Bauhaus, Gropius worked in the office of which German architect, alongside Mies van der Rohe and Le Corbusier?
questions.n: Behrens is considered the first 'industrial designer' and his office served as the training ground for the greatest masters of the Modern movement.

questions.q: Which factory building, designed by Gropius and Adolf Meyer in 1911, is famous for its 'curtain wall' of glass and lack of visible corner supports?
questions.n: The shoe-last factory's transparent corners were a revolutionary step toward the weightless aesthetic of Modern architecture.

questions.q: After fleeing Nazi Germany, Gropius became the chairman of the Department of Architecture at which prestigious American university?
questions.n: His tenure at Harvard effectively exported Bauhaus ideals to the United States, influencing generations of American architects.

questions.q: What is the name of the collaborative architectural firm Gropius founded in the United States in 1945?
questions.n: TAC embodied Gropius's belief in teamwork over individual 'stardom', a core tenet of his philosophy.

questions.q: What was Gropius’s personal residence in Lincoln, Massachusetts, which blended Bauhaus principles with New England regional traditions?
questions.n: The house used industrial materials like glass block and chrome alongside traditional local materials like fieldstone and white vertical siding.

questions.q: The Bauhaus Dessau is famous for its 'pinwheel' plan. What does this mean in terms of its spatial organization?
questions.n: The building's wings radiate from a core without a central axis, making it impossible to see the whole building from one single viewpoint.

questions.q: What is the term for the vast, non-load-bearing glass facade used in the workshop wing to allow maximum light into the interior?
questions.n: This feature allowed for the 'dissolution of the wall,' a hallmark of International Style architecture.

questions.q: How are the different functions (dormitories, workshops, classrooms) connected in the Dessau building?
questions.n: A two-story bridge structure spans across the road, physically linking the administrative and workshop areas.

questions.q: The interior used a specific color palette to identify different zones. Who was the Bauhaus master in charge of the wall-painting workshop?
questions.n: Scheper's work involved using color as a spatial tool to differentiate walls, ceilings, and structural elements.

questions.q: What type of roof was used for the Bauhaus building, which was a controversial departure from traditional German pitched roofs?
questions.n: The flat roof represented modern technology and provided additional usable space for the students.

questions.q: What is the name of the iconic Art Deco skyscraper in New York featuring a 'sunburst' spire made of Nirosta stainless steel?
questions.n: Designed by William van Alen, it was briefly the tallest building in the world and is a masterpiece of Art Deco ornament.

questions.q: Art Deco often used 'stepped' forms on high-rise buildings. What was the legal driver for this architectural shape in New York?
questions.n: To prevent skyscrapers from blocking light and air to the streets below, buildings were required to 'step back' as they got taller.

questions.q: Which sub-style of Art Deco is characterized by rounded corners, horizontal grooves (speed lines), and a nautical appearance?
questions.n: This later phase of Art Deco was influenced by aerodynamics and the look of ocean liners and fast trains.

questions.q: In the Philippines, which university campus is famous for having the largest collection of Art Deco buildings, designed by Pablo Antonio?
questions.n: The campus remains a cohesive example of the style and is a National Cultural Treasure.

questions.q: Art Deco ornamentation often drew from which ancient civilization, following the discovery of King Tutankhamun’s tomb in 1922?
questions.n: Stylized lotuses, papyrus, and solar discs became popular decorative motifs in Art Deco buildings.

questions.q: Neoclassical Revival is characterized by the use of a 'colonnade' or 'portico.' What is a Portico?
o: A row of windows near the ceiling
A porch leading to the entrance of a building, or covered by a walkway with columns and a pediment.
A tower located at the corner of a building
questions.n: The portico creates a grand, formal transition between the street and the interior.

questions.q: What is the term for the heavy, protruding masonry blocks at the corners of Neoclassical buildings used to provide a sense of strength?
questions.n: These elements reinforce the corners visually and structurally, creating a sense of permanence and weight.

questions.q: In Neoclassical facades, windows are often topped with alternating 'triangular' and 'segmental' versions of what feature?
questions.n: Derived from temple architecture, these window pediments add rhythmic detail to the facade.

questions.q: Which British architect was a leading figure of the Neoclassical style and designed the Bank of England?
questions.n: Known for his inventive use of light and space, his own house is now a museum of Neoclassical and eclectic artifacts.

questions.q: Neoclassical Revival was the official style for many Philippine colonial buildings under the Americans. What is the name of the 'Plan' that dictated this style for Manila?
questions.n: Daniel Burnham's 1905 plan intended to turn Manila into a 'modern' city with wide boulevards and Neoclassical civic centers.
